sections.body_en:
The trait of faith is the heritage of all human beings. As stated above (1:1), through faith a person relies on his senses and his intellect, on his family members and his friends. Through it he believes that his life has meaning, and he plans his future with hope and confidence that he will succeed in improving his life for the better. Through it he believes that there are values worth striving for, such as the values of truth and goodness. On a higher level, a person by his nature believes that there is a supreme and eternal power above everything that is seen, by whose power all things exist, and by whose power all values have a supreme and sacred worth. And his personal life, too, is bound up with eternity, and its worth is greater than the mundane and fleeting routine of his life on earth. To give expression to this faith, all human societies created religions for themselves.

Let us explain further: faith is the foundation of man's existence in the world, for upon it his cognition and consciousness rest. Beyond this, man lives in an unstable world, with dangers lurking all around him. Nothing that sustains him is guaranteed: if he does not work diligently and store up food and property, he may die of hunger; if he does not take the trouble to store water, he may die of thirst. He must build himself a house to protect himself from cold and heat and from beasts of prey. He also needs an organized society to protect himself from thieves and enemies who might plunder his property and enslave or exploit him. In order to secure himself against illness and old age, and to merit a continuity that has in it a kind of eternity, he establishes a family and has children. And still, after all the toil, nothing is guaranteed. Without faith that life has value and that the effort is worthwhile, he would despair, and his chances of survival would diminish. He also senses that this faith which drives him has its source in the stable and eternal Source of life, which he defines as God. And he understands that the more he is filled with faith in God, the more he will merit confidence and stability, diligence and resourcefulness. Especially in times of distress, when a threat looms over his life, such as in times of illness, famine or war, he turns to God in prayer and asks for His help, and he is strengthened in faith to act to save himself, his family, his friends and his people.

But it is not only the need to survive that impels a person to connect to his God, but even more so the desire to progress, to break through boundaries and to rise without end, and to give his life eternal meaning. This is what is stated (Bereshit 1:27): "And God created man in His image; in the image of God He created him." Since he was created in the "image of God," his inner nature has no boundaries, and his aspirations are without limit. Therefore, even when a person attains stability he does not rest, for out of his natural faith he always aspires to more: to understand more, to feel more, to enjoy more, to create and develop more. For there is no end to his aspiration to understand the world, to his longing to experience all the beauty and sublimity in the world, to his yearning to delight in all the pleasantness and goodness in the world, and to his desire to create and develop his world with the help of his talents. And when he delves into his soul, he understands that the more closely he is bound to God, the more he will realize his yearning and increase his blessing, and everything he attains and develops will be of greater value. That is to say, man, by the nature of his creation, yearns for closeness to God, to the infinite Source of all the aspirations for which he longs.

As stated, man's aspiration is infinite, and because of this an immense yearning to draw close to God is aroused in him. But an immense problem stands before him: since God is infinite, He cannot be defined, and without definition it is hard to draw close to Him. If he is wise and upright, he will restrain himself with strength and understand that God is above and beyond all comprehension, and out of humility he will try to receive inspiration from Him, to walk in His ways and to add blessing to the world. But many are tempted to define and corporealize God, to see Him reflected in the great forces of creation, such as heaven and earth, the sun, the moon and the stars, the sea and the wind, the animal, vegetable and mineral realms. And since values and created things are many, a person is tempted to see all the forces, qualities and values as various and numerous idols, such as a "god of truth" revealed in the sun, by whose light things become clear, a "god of war" revealed in the stormy wind, and a "god of fertility" revealed in the soil or in the rain. Over time, in a gradual process, men of spirit and art created statues and images that symbolized the forces of nature and the great values, and created modes of worship through which a person could give honor to the idols and merit their closeness and their blessing. In this way all the various idolatrous religions came into being.

Let us explain further: many people at times merit a mystical spiritual experience, in which they suddenly merit a great illumination above and beyond what is familiar to them, and they feel that this illumination elevates them and gives inspiration to their lives, and they want to give it a permanent place in their lives. But after the illumination departs, since they have no words or language to describe it, it gradually fades until it is forgotten, and only a vague yearning and longing for that great experience remains. Special are the men of spirit who merit to experience these spiritual experiences with greater intensity and frequency, until they feel that they have encountered the source of their life and their soul, which is grasped in their consciousness as God, and it becomes clear to them that God gives life to the world and gives meaning to their lives, and that it is for Him that they have always longed. At times, within this illumination, they feel that heaven and earth are uniting, that past and future are merging, and questions about the meaning of life are resolved for them, and they foresee the future. After the experience passes, they are not willing to give it up, and they know that the more they succeed in storing it in their consciousness and recreating it, the more they will intensify their lives. And then a great choice stands before them. If they gird themselves with humility and patience, they will absorb the spiritual experience in its purity, and in a deep and gradual process it will elevate them to become seekers of truth and kindness. And if they continue to refine themselves, to rise higher and to increase good deeds, they will merit the holy spirit, with the help of which they will be able to pave paths for the repair of character and deeds. But in many, the temptation to experience the spiritual experience again, and soon, with all their senses, prevailed, and using their spiritual, literary and artistic talent, they corporealized the deity and defined it and its character, and created images, statues and modes of worship for it.

The basis of the idolatrous error is that God indeed gives life to everything, and in all the forces of nature, in man and in animals, a Divine spark is revealed that gives them life. And men of spirit and art are capable of grasping this spark as standing on its own, and of giving it the tangible form of a statue, and of creating around it modes of worship that are supposed to give a person the possibility of recreating the spiritual experiences and receiving inspiration from them. The rites included offering sacrifices, song and dance, harlotry, drugs and alcohol. When they succeeded in creating a statue and modes of worship that made a great impression and echoed the spiritual experience hidden in people's hearts, an idolatrous cult was created that intensified the feeling of faith within them, and gave them strength and confidence, and hope that by virtue of their worship of the idol they would merit blessing.

The advantage of idolatry is that it gives people a strong feeling of closeness to the great forces in the world, and stirs hearts with tremendous intensity that seemingly expresses the meaning of life. The disadvantage is that it lies: the forces that its statues represent, and to which people connect, are created forces. And the true way to draw close to God, who is their source, and to merit His blessing, is by walking in His ways through the repair of thought, character and deeds, and not by worshipping the forces that the statues represent.

sections.title_en: Without Faith in God, People Believe in Idols
sections.body_en:
As we have learned, man by nature believes, and if he does not believe in the true God, he will tend to believe in idolatry. For man's natural faith also includes the belief that there is an explanation and meaning for what happens in nature and for what happens to man, and it also includes the belief that there is a way by which a person can solve his distress and advance himself. Therefore, even when he does not find a well-founded explanation for what happens in nature and to man, he will believe that there is an explanation, and will accept the explanation that seems most logical to him, even though it is not properly founded. Thus, out of a basic assumption of faith, men of spirit created the idolatrous religions, which gave an explanation and meaning for what happens in the world and to man, and they developed rites through which they could merit the favor of the idols. In our day their faith seems ridiculous, but in past eras, given the reality of man's life in the shadow of the mighty forces of nature, and given man's natural faith, the idolatrous conception seemed inevitable. There could indeed be different interpretations of the higher powers, but all of them were idolatrous. Therefore there were no deep differences between the various idolatrous religions, and everywhere an idolatrous interpretation was given to reality, in accordance with the conditions of life and the environment.

This nature of man, to seek an explanation and to believe in it, is positive at its foundation, and stems from the image of God in man, that is, from his believing in his ability to understand the world and to act to change it for the better. By virtue of this faith, a person believes that it is worth making the effort to find a solution to every problem. But the evil inclination turns this trait toward believing in false solutions and falling into terrible errors. In the end, however, a person will understand that as a result of his error his troubles and afflictions have increased, and he will continue to search, and by virtue of this he will continue to progress. This trait causes even today people suffering from an incurable disease to run after false remedies, and to be willing to pay enormous sums for them, for by their nature they believe that there is a solution to their problem, and therefore they are tempted to believe in the various solutions offered to them. In the world of scientific medicine as well, there are diseases for which no effective treatment has been found, and yet it is accepted to give them treatment of little benefit. For doctors too, like other human beings, believe by their nature that there must be a solution to problems, and when there is no solution, they are willing to make do with a solution whose chances are low rather than face the painful recognition that there is no solution. Moreover, the belief that the remedy can heal also has the power to help, as has been found that when a person takes a pill that he believes will heal him, even though there is nothing in it, it affects his recovery in a certain percentage of cases (the "placebo" effect).

Only exceptional individuals, possessing humility and integrity, are capable, as long as they have no well-founded answer, of restraining themselves and saying "I do not know," and continuing to search for a solution, while being willing to pay a price for it. Thanks to them science develops. So too with faith: only exceptional individuals were able to restrain themselves and say, "Although I know with certainty that there is a supreme Source of the world, I know nothing about it," and not to compromise by accepting partial explanations that are not properly founded and do not accord with their moral aspiration to add goodness and blessing to the world. That is to say, people of small faith accept a partial explanation that seems best for them, and are satisfied with the moral level accepted in society and do not strive for more. And people of great faith believe that there is a higher answer, and therefore they are not satisfied with the partial answer and with the moral level accepted in society, and they wait until a better answer is revealed to them that will raise their moral level.

Unique was Avraham Avinu, who, because of the greatness of his faith, would not compromise and accept any explanation containing a trace of idolatry and corporealization or an infringement of morality. He was even prepared to give his life for this, until he merited that the Lord, Creator of the world, appeared to him and made a covenant with him that from his descendants a blessed people would arise, which would walk in the ways of God, inherit the Land of Israel, and add goodness and blessing to the world. Later, God appeared to His people Israel in a general prophetic revelation and gave them His Torah, containing guidance for cleaving to faith in God's unity and for the repair of man and the world and their redemption. From then on an entire people could walk in the ways of God, cleave to faith in God's unity and reject idolatry, and the Divine light began to be revealed in the world. In a long and winding process, the people of Israel succeeded in abolishing crude idolatry from the world. And still a long road lies before them: to abolish also the subtle idolatry that inclines a person to believe in religions that contain a little idolatry, or in partial technological and social solutions, and to reveal the Divine light in its purity, and to repair the world under the kingship of the Almighty.

By his nature, man believes that there is truth and falsehood, good and evil, and that it is fitting for a person to cleave to truth and goodness and to distance himself from falsehood and evil. The question is what is truth and what is falsehood, what is good and what is evil, and to what extent a person must strive to cleave to truth and goodness. The answers to these questions depend on his general conception of faith regarding the source of life and the way the world is conducted. The more crudely a person describes faith, as idolatrous forces whose image and character are drawn from nature, the less moral he becomes. For the human moral idea, which stems from his having been created in the image of God, is not reflected in nature; on the contrary, in nature it appears that the strong survive; the strong animals overpower the weak and devour them. The forces of nature, too, act arbitrarily. Suddenly a storm erupts and a flood of rain drowns people and animals, and lightning causes fires and death; and at times the heavens are shut and give no rain upon the earth, and the tree withers and the grain does not grow, and man and beast die of hunger and thirst.

The corporealization of God also necessitates splitting faith into many gods, for in the physical world many forces are revealed, and to represent them many idols must be created. By the way of nature these idols compete and fight with one another, just as the forces of nature, animals and different peoples fight with one another. In continuation of this, the conception becomes established among men that war and competition are the nature of the world, and that it is the nature of the strong to overpower the weak and enslave or exploit them.

Thus it came about that those who sinned through idolatry debased faith, and created a destructive combination between the feeling of faith and man's arrogance and lust. Instead of faith elevating man's aspirations to cleave to truth and morality, and thereby changing his character for the better and improving his ways so that he would add goodness and blessing to the world, idolatry gave meaning and justification to man as he is, with all his evil inclinations, and thereby became an instrument meant to glorify his desires and pleasures. In doing so, idolatry blocked the way of faith in God's unity to elevate the world and repair it. For as a rule, the idol worshipper does not aspire to improve in the moral sense, but to quench his thirst for a spiritual experience that will give flavor to his life, and to satisfy his needs and lusts. For this purpose he offers sacrifices, whispers incantations, and performs magical acts that will help him grow rich, defeat his enemies, attain tranquility, and obtain everything he wants.

Indeed, there are levels among the worshippers of idolatry, and whenever the men of spirit and art were called upon to describe the idolatrous faith and to arrange modes of worship for it, a choice stood before them: whether they would strengthen wickedness by corporealizing faith and describing the gods as possessed of lusts, desiring to conquer and rule with almost no regard for the values of truth and justice; or whether they would remember the supreme root of all the powers, and describe the idols also as possessing good spiritual qualities, as aspiring to truth and justice, and as loving to do good and to show mercy. To the extent that conscience remained in their hearts, inspired by the abstract supreme Source, they associated the name of Heaven with their worship and chose to describe the gods in a more spiritual and moral manner, and thereby influenced people to be better, and thus advanced the world in a positive direction. The masses who worshipped idols also faced a choice: whether to connect to the base aspects in the description of the idols, or to the moral aspects that were hidden to a certain degree in the idolatrous descriptions.

Above all this, the faith of Israel is faith in the One God, who is the sole source of all life and of all moral values, which give life great and uplifting meaning without limit.1

notes_en.en:
In order to understand the meaning of the great war of the Torah of Israel against idolatry, let us tell a little about the idols and their characteristics. It should be prefaced that the priests of religion were talented people with lofty insights, and with various images they succeeded in giving convincing definitions to the Divine forces revealed in the world, and in sweeping the masses to connect to them with tremendous intensity. Therefore, although the stories of the religions' myths seem ridiculous today, in those times they seemed dictated by reality. But in Israel, even then, they described them with mockery, as the Torah commands (below 14:1).
All the idolatrous religions, such as the Egyptian, the Babylonian, the Canaanite, the Assyrian, the Persian and the Greek, had a series of idols (a pantheon), each of the gods having its own characteristics. These idols represented various forces that exist in nature and in the human soul, forces that drive what happens in the world. Some of the gods tended to do good and to show mercy, but most of them did not excel in morality, and the strong idols were those that were willing to murder, lie, betray and kill their relatives, including their parents; yet in them too good qualities sparkled from time to time. (See further below 9:1.)
Zeus, the strong Greek god, was the sixth son born to the pair of gods Kronos and Rhea. But since Kronos had a prophecy that one of his sons would depose him, he took care to swallow all his children. This grieved his wife Rhea, and when she gave birth to her sixth son, she gave her husband Kronos a stone wrapped in cloth instead of her son. Kronos swallowed the stone, and the infant Zeus grew up in secret until he succeeded in tricking his father, who did not recognize him, and in the course of a great war among the gods, he overcame his father, cut him into a thousand pieces, and was appointed supreme ruler of the gods. Thus it was not because of his moral virtues that he acquired his status, but because he was strong and fate stood by his side. Zeus married his sister Hera, who was jealous and vengeful, and with her he fathered various gods. Zeus was known as a lecher, a drunkard, and a pursuer of goddesses and women, and from them he fathered more kinds of gods and demigods. He was also hot-tempered and wrathful, but when sacrifices were offered to him, he tended to be appeased.
According to the Babylonian story, the ancient and great god Apsu became angry at the lesser gods, who celebrated, made noise and disturbed his rest, and therefore he decided to destroy them. But this was revealed to them, and they succeeded in tricking him and killing him. Then two other gods reigned. In time, Apsu's widow, Tiamat, wanted to avenge him, and she made an alliance with various monsters in order to destroy the noisy gods. All the gods were then very afraid, but Marduk, who was Tiamat's grandson, volunteered to go out against her in battle, on condition that if he won he would reign over them all. He succeeded in killing Tiamat, dismembered her corpse, and created from it heaven and earth. In time, the gods saw that the work was hard for them, and therefore they decided to create human beings who would work for them. Since then they amuse themselves and fulfill their lusts, while human beings work in their place, serve them, and offer them sacrifices to satisfy their hunger.
In the Canaanite story, the creator of the world is called "El," and his wife is "Asherah." They bore Ba'al, Ashtoret, Anat, Yam, Mot and other gods. "Ba'al" was the god of rain who fertilizes the soil, and he married "Ashtoret." "Yam" was the god of the seas and rivers, and "Mot" the god of death. "El" decided that "Yam" would inherit his place as ruler of the gods, but "Ba'al" opposed this, and together with "Anat," the goddess of war, waged war against him, at the end of which he killed "Yam." That is to say, in the lands under Ba'al's rule, the rain gives life to the soil, and not the river as in Egypt and Babylon. Afterward the god "Mot" killed "Ba'al" and brought him down to the netherworld, until his sister "Anat" brought him up from the netherworld back to the throne. The meaning of this is that every year, when summer arrives, "Ba'al" dies and descends to the netherworld, that is, the rain passes, and when winter arrives he comes back to life and returns to fertilize the soil. Similarly, every idolatrous religion had a series of idols suited to its land and its living conditions: some central, which were worshipped more, and some secondary, which were worshipped in special situations in which their help could be of use.

sections.body_en:
Let us continue to delve into the difference between the true faith, which is the Israelite faith in God's unity, and faith in idols. In faith in God's unity, God is the source of goodness and justice, and the various powers are meant to serve goodness and justice. Likewise, the purpose of man, who was created in the image of God, is to walk in the ways of God, to do righteousness and justice, to add blessing to the world and to bring about its repair. Therefore the believer in God wants human beings to cooperate with one another, to love and help one another, and not to deceive one another, and that no person exploit his fellow's distress in order to withhold his wages or rob him; thereby welfare and abundance will be added to society as a whole, and the general good in the world will increase.

By contrast, in idolatrous faith there is a separation between morality and power, and since, according to the corporealizing conception, power is more prominent and influential, it is more important. And just as the idols use their power to satisfy their lusts, so human beings who have gained power under their patronage are permitted to use it as they please, and to enjoy all the good there is in the world without striving to cultivate it for the benefit of the public and of future generations.

For example, if bored gods enjoy sending thunder and stirring up storms at sea, and amuse themselves by hearing the cries of sailors about to drown at sea, then rulers too are permitted to amuse themselves with the cries of the people they torment for having dared to defy their command. By contrast, in Israel the Sages instituted a blessing over storms and thunder: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, whose power and might fill the world," to teach us that storms and thunder are from God, and that they are meant to arouse us to fear of Heaven and to good deeds. For "thunder was created only to straighten the crookedness of the heart, as it is stated (Kohelet 3:14): 'And God has made it so, that men should fear before Him'" (Berakhot 59b).

According to the faith of Israel, rulers are forbidden to exploit their authority for evil. Therefore the king of Israel, who possesses the greatest governing power, is commanded to write for himself a Torah scroll that will always be with him and guide him on the straight path, and he is commanded not to pride himself on many horses, and not to be drawn after his lust by multiplying silver and wives. Likewise judges are forbidden to take bribes and pervert judgment. By contrast, among the worshippers of idolatry, only the weak needed to obey all the rules, but those with power did not see themselves as bound by the rules, and they exploited their status to receive bribes and increase their wealth, just as the idols too receive bribes and help whoever offered sacrifices to them. Therefore criminals for whom calamity was decided would run to the altars of the idols, and as long as they held on to the altar, they could not be punished, so as not to arouse the idol's wrath. But in Israel it is a mitzva to punish the criminal even if he takes hold of the horns of the altar, as it is stated (Shemot 21:14): "And if a man acts presumptuously against his fellow, to kill him with guile, from My altar you shall take him to die," for God hates wickedness and flattery.

Therefore the Torah called the prohibition of idol worship harlotry, as it is stated: "And this people will rise up and go astray (zana) after the foreign gods of the land" (Devarim 31:16), and it is stated: "For they went astray (zanu) after other gods and bowed down to them" (Shofetim 2:17). For just as harlotry separates selfish lust, which is meant to satisfy the inclinations, from faithful love, which is the foundation of the true existence of life, so idol worship separates truth and morality from power, and instead of power serving truth and morality, which are the foundation of life, it is used for the satisfaction of lusts, which are the opposite of love.

Since power was in their eyes the supreme value, the idols did not keep faith with one another, but used to choose the winning side. Similarly, the idol worshippers were not faithful to their idols, but needed their power; and when they felt that their idol was failing them and not helping them, they would switch to worshipping another idol that seemed to them stronger and more successful. Sometimes, in order to flatter the new one, they would even despise their previous idol and smash its image. And sometimes the priests of the idol that had failed succeeded in persuading the people that their idol was indeed going through a difficult period, but that its powers were about to return to it, and then it would reward whoever had believed in it in its difficult hour, and severely punish those who had despised it.

Generally, the idol worshippers would appease their idols with offerings of plants or animals, which expressed man's devotion and submission to the idols. But at times, when it seemed to them that the regular sacrifices were not sufficient to satisfy the gods' will, they offered them human sacrifices, in order to appease the gods' wrath or to restrain their desire to sow destruction. Likewise, at times after a victory in war, the victors offered human sacrifices to the gods, so that the idols would not suspect them of being arrogant and forgetting their lowly status and punish them severely. In this context, the rulers could choose to sacrifice the people who were less desirable to them, and likewise parents who sacrificed their children could choose a baby who cried a lot or a sickly child. Indeed, at times, when they feared a severe calamity, they sacrificed what was dear to them, for they feared that otherwise the gods would destroy everyone in their wrath. An example is Mesha king of Moav, who, at a time of danger from a severe siege, sacrificed his firstborn son: "And he took his firstborn son, who was to reign in his stead, and offered him up as a burnt offering upon the wall" (II Melakhim 3:27). There were idols whose believers offered them many human sacrifices, such as the Molekh and the gods of Sefarvayim. The Sages said that the Molekh was a statue with the face of a calf, which had two hands, beneath which a great fire burned; and the parents of the babies, or the priests of the Molekh, would place the baby in a bowl on the two hands of the statue until it was burned to death. So as not to hear its screams of crying, the priests of the idols would beat drums. At times the idol worshippers even slaughtered their parents to the gods, as Rabbi Akiva testified: "I saw a gentile who bound his father and offered him before his object of worship" (Otzar Midrashim; see Sifrei, Re'eh 81). Against all this, the Torah warned Israel not to learn from the ways of the Canaanites, "for every abomination to the Lord, which He hates, they have done for their gods; for they even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire to their gods" (Devarim 12:31).

The more crude the idolatrous conception was, the more evil the rites it created, which helped their worshippers cleave to the forces of life in their base form and intensify them. Many rites included harlotry, in order to arouse the gods to bestow blessing upon the soil and the crops. In the Canaanite religion, for example, "Ba'al," the god of rain, was male, and his wife "Ashtoret" was the goddess of beauty and fertility. In addition to offering sacrifices and burning incense on their altars to appease them, the priests of "Ba'al" would have relations with various women in order to arouse "Ba'al" to bestow rain upon them, and the priestesses of "Ashtoret" would give themselves to various men in order to arouse "Ashtoret" to bestow beauty and fertility upon them. "Asherah" was the mother of Ba'al and Ashtoret, and she too was sometimes worshipped through adultery, as it is written (I Melakhim 14:23-24): "For they also built for themselves high places, and pillars, and asherim, on every high hill and under every leafy tree. And there were also kadesh (harlotry) in the land; they did according to all the abominations of the nations that the Lord had driven out before the Children of Israel" (see Avoda Zara 44a regarding Ma'akha). In Greece, the worship of the god Dionysus, god of the vine and of wine, included mass revelry and harlotry. And the worship of Aphrodite, goddess of beauty and love, included the abandonment of virgins in her temple, with the etnan (the harlot's fee) being paid to the temple of Aphrodite.

Beyond the terrible sins involved in idolatry, it also prevents a person from the possibility of repenting and improving morally. For according to the idolatrous conception, people justified the way and the deeds of wicked rulers who murdered, plundered and enslaved, since they were following the way of the strong idols, who ruled and fulfilled their lusts by means of murder, falsehood, adultery, plunder and enslavement.

In ancient times, before the influence of the people of Israel spread in the world, almost all human beings worshipped idols and believed that they helped them, saving them from calamity and increasing their wealth and health. Jews also sinned in this, and so we find that the prophet Yirmeyahu (44:1-14) rebuked those who went down to Egypt after the destruction of the Temple: if, after they had worshipped idolatry and been punished with destruction, killing, famine and exile, they continued to worship the "Queen of Heaven" in Egypt, no remnant or survivor of them would remain to return to the land of Yehuda. But they answered him insolently that precisely at the time they had worshipped idolatry in Jerusalem they had enjoyed good fortune: "And we had plenty of bread, and were well, and saw no evil. But since we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out libations to her, we have lacked everything, and have been consumed by the sword and by famine" (Yirmeyahu 44:17-18).

Some explain that the success described by the idol worshippers stemmed from the psychological reinforcement they received from their faith, which gave them confidence that what they wanted was indeed good and just, for they were not acting in their own name alone, but under the patronage of the idols, who justified their aspirations and helped them by virtue of the sacrifices they had offered them. From their perspective, this was not an invented faith, because faith is ingrained in man and spurs him to explain reality and give it meaning. And since their idolatrous conception grew out of the deep and powerful experiences they had, and out of contemplation of the great forces in nature and in man, the idolatrous explanation of what happens in the world was, from their perspective, inevitable.

Beyond this, many explain that just as there are forces of nature in the world that man can harness for his needs, so above them there are spiritual forces, called angels and demons, that operate the forces of nature (see below 19:5-8). And deep men of spirit are capable of grasping their essence and their modes of operation, and by means of idolatrous rites of connecting to them and drawing power from them in order to increase their property and status, or to turn them against their enemies. So the Torah relates that Balak king of Moav turned to the wicked Bil'am with a request that he curse Israel, "for I know that whom you bless is blessed, and whom you curse is cursed" (Bemidbar 22:6). The Sages said (Sanhedrin 105b) that Bil'am knew how to pinpoint the moment when there is Divine anger in the world, and to direct it through his curse at whomever he wished. But in the end his curse was turned into a blessing for Israel, and he himself lost his life in this world and in the World to Come. And so it happens to all idol worshippers: even when they succeed in activating the forces of nature as forces of impurity cut off from their root, in the end the forces of nature reconnect to their source and lead to their downfall.

sections.title_en: The Forces of Impurity and Their Falsehood
sections.body_en:
The great figures of Israel disagreed about the explanations we learned in the previous section. Some say that the idols had no influence at all, and everything was in people's imagination, based on the beliefs and lies spread by the priests of the religions. This was the view of the Rambam. And some say that the idolatrous rites did have an influence on what happens in the world, but that this was done through the forces of impurity. This was the view of the Ramban and many others. Both views have sources in the Tanakh and in the words of the Sages.

On the one hand, we learn in the Torah that Bil'am had the power to curse and to bless, but God turned his curse into a blessing for Israel (Bemidbar 22:6; Devarim 23:6). Likewise we learn that Pharaoh had magicians who, with the help of sorcery, could cast down their staffs and turn them into serpents, but Aharon's staff swallowed their staffs, for God rules over all (Shemot 7:11-12). And so we find in the words of the Sages that sorcerers had the power to influence what happens in the world (Sanhedrin 67b, and elsewhere).

On the other hand, when the prophets of Israel rebuked Israel to cleave to God and merit blessing and not to stray after the idols, they determined decisively that the idols are falsehood and have no benefit whatsoever: "which cannot profit or save, for they are vain" (I Shmuel 12:21). "They walked after things that do not profit" (Yirmeyahu 2:5). "What profit is the carved image, that its maker has carved it… to make mute idols… Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all within it" (Ḥavakuk 2:18-19). Likewise the prophet Yeshayahu (44:6-20) mocked the idol worshippers, who took wood, roasted meat on half of it and made a statue from the other half, and bowed down and prayed to it as if it could help. And it is likewise stated (Tehillim 115:4-7): "Their idols (the statues of the nations) are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but do not speak; they have eyes but do not see. They have ears but do not hear; they have noses but do not smell. Their hands do not feel, their feet do not walk; they make no sound in their throat."

It seems that one can explain that mystical forces do indeed exist, with whose help idol worshippers and sorcerers sometimes succeed in foreseeing the future and influencing nature. But in the overall reckoning they do not gain; on the contrary, they lose. For whoever relies on them gives up, to a certain degree, the intellectual effort to plan his ways, and since the predictions they make are not precise, in practice whoever makes use of them errs more. Thus it turns out that the magical blessing that comes through them is always less than the blessing that stems from diligence based on correct thinking and planning. Therefore, although on the one hand there were people who, with the help of idolatrous rites, succeeded in foreseeing the future and changing things in the world, in the overall reckoning they lost. Hence, on the one hand, one can accept the conception that the spiritual forces of impurity in idolatrous rites have an influence on reality; but on the other hand, one can say that everything is falsehood, since in practice, in the overall reckoning, no blessing grew from them.

Similarly, one can say that hard and dangerous drugs give whoever takes them temporary happiness, but that in the long run they are bad and harmful; and on the other hand, one can say that they give no happiness at all, because in the overall reckoning they deplete the powers of the soul and the body and cause suffering and death.2

notes_en.en:
When the prophets rebuked Israel, they determined that there is no benefit whatsoever in the idols (I Shmuel 12:21; Yeshayahu 44; Yirmeyahu 2; and elsewhere). On the other hand, we find that the Torah attributes real powers to sorcerers and magicians, in Egypt (Shemot 7:11-12), and in the story of the woman who consulted the dead (I Shmuel 28). Likewise, the Sages relate to demons as a fact (Berakhot 6a; Yevamot 122a; and elsewhere), and likewise to sorcery (Sanhedrin 67b). We further find in Daniel and in the words of Ḥazal that the nations are subject to the influence of angels ("princes") (Daniel 10:20; Yoma 77a). In Sanhedrin 90a they disagreed about this: "Rabbi Abahu said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: In every matter, if a prophet tells you to transgress the words of the Torah, listen to him, except for idolatry; for even if he makes the sun stand still for you in the middle of the sky, do not listen to him. It was taught: Rabbi Yosei Ha-Gelili says: The Torah reached the depth of the mind of idolatry (that they are able to perform wonders); therefore the Torah gave dominion over it, that even if he makes the sun stand still for you in the middle of the sky, do not listen to him. It was taught: Rabbi Akiva said: Heaven forbid that the Holy One, blessed be He, would make the sun stand still for those who transgress His will. Rather, it refers to one such as Ḥananya ben Azur, who was at first a true prophet and in the end a false prophet" (and therefore he was able to perform a wonder). And see below, section 10, that the Sages described cases in which idolatrous practices appeared to be effective.
The view of the great majority of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim is that there is substance to these spiritual forces, but the Torah forbade turning to them (Ramban, Devarim 4:19; 18:9; Rabbeinu Baḥya, ibid. 18:10; Sefer Ha-ikkarim 3:8; Ran, Derashot 4 and 12; Rivash 92; Abarbanel, Devarim 18; Radbaz 3:405; Ramḥal in Ma'amar Ha-ikkarim; Gra, YD 179:13; and many others; and see below 19:5).
On the other hand, on the basis of the words of the prophets in the verses cited above and in other places, the Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:16; Moreh Nevukhim 3:37; Commentary on the Mishna, Avoda Zara 4:7) explained at length that all matters of sorcery and divination are vanity, and that the Torah forbade them in order to distance Israel from engaging in these falsehoods, after which those lacking understanding are drawn, but the wise know with clear proofs that they are vanity. And so wrote the Meiri (Avoda Zara 54b; Sanhedrin 101a). According to the Radak (Yirmeyahu 14:14) and the Ma'aseh Roke'aḥ (on Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:16), the Rambam too agrees that there is substance to these forces, but they are vanity and deceit because they mix lies with truth, since they come from the forces of impurity. And so it is somewhat implied in Moreh Nevukhim 2:37 and in his introduction to the Mishna. And although the Rambam would not necessarily agree with what is explained above, it seems that this is the explanation that takes into account the words of all of them and expresses the view of most of the Sages of Israel.

sections.body_en:
Although many agree that there are idol worshippers or sorcerers who sometimes succeed in influencing reality in a magical way or in foreseeing the future, in practice even those special people do not succeed in reproducing their power consistently. Sometimes, while they were still innocent and humble, they merited a number of mystical experiences and succeeded in bringing things about magically; but after they became famous, they had difficulty reproducing those experiences and magical abilities. And since they greatly yearn for this, even though they are not sure whether they succeeded, they tend to deceive themselves and imagine that they did indeed have a certain mystical experience through which they succeeded in influencing reality or foreseeing the future. And if they did so with the help of impressive ceremonies accompanied by alcohol or drugs, they could convince themselves of this more easily.

And some knew that they had no magical powers, but in order to receive the money and honor that believers bestow on the priests of the idols and on sorcerers, they learned to conduct the ceremonies and to create the impression that they were capable of influencing reality, and they prophesied in vague and ambiguous language, so that they could always claim that they had succeeded in foreseeing the future. Often they also convinced themselves that their lies were justified, for thereby they were helping suffering people, and without a religious framework society would fall apart.

Sometimes the lies of the idol worshippers were blatant. As the Sages related: when the prophet Eliyahu told King Aḥav to gather all the people to Mount Carmel, and the four hundred and fifty prophets of Ba'al would stand opposite him, and each would pray to his god to bring down fire on his sacrifice, so that the people would see that the Lord is God, and only He can bring down fire from heaven, a man named Ḥiel, on behalf of the priests of Ba'al, prepared a hollow altar and went in underneath it, so that when the prophets of Ba'al cried out to Ba'al to bring down fire for them, he would light a fire from below. But by Divine providence, while he was lying under the altar, a snake bit him and he died. Thus, when the prophets of Ba'al cried out to their idol to bring down fire for them, Ḥiel could not hear their voices and light the fire. Thinking that he had fallen asleep, they raised their cries, but the cries no longer woke him. Afterward, when Eliyahu offered his sacrifice to God, fire came down from heaven, and it became known that the Lord is God (I Melakhim 18; Yalkut Shimoni 214).

sections.title_en: The Free Choice to Believe in Idols
sections.body_en:
The purpose of man's creation is that, by the power of his free choice, he will choose the good. Therefore God left room for man to believe in Him with pure faith and thereby rise higher and merit blessing, or to err and worship idols, which are created forces, and lose his world.

Similarly, the Sages said (Avoda Zara 54b): "The philosophers asked the elders (the Jewish elders) in Rome: If your God does not desire idol worship, why does He not abolish it? They said to them: If they worshipped something the world does not need, He would abolish it. But they worship the sun, the moon, the stars and the constellations. Shall He destroy the world because of the fools?! Rather, the world follows its natural course, and the fools who acted corruptly will in the future have to give an accounting." An example of this: "Suppose a man stole a se'a of wheat and went and sowed it in the ground. By right it should not grow (for how could a sinner profit?), but the world follows its natural course, and the fools who acted corruptly will in the future have to give an accounting." Another example of this: "Suppose a man had relations with his fellow's wife. By right she should not conceive, but the world follows its natural course, and the fools who acted corruptly will in the future have to give an accounting."

The Sages further said (Avoda Zara 55a): Zunin said to Rabbi Akiva: My heart and your heart know that there is no substance to idolatry, but there is a difficulty: we see sick people who go to a house of idolatry, and when they come out they are healthy. "He said to him: I will tell you a parable. To what is the matter comparable? To a trustworthy man who was in a city, and all the people of his city would deposit (money) with him without witnesses. One man came and deposited with him in the presence of witnesses (because he did not trust him). Once he forgot and deposited with him without witnesses. His wife said to him: Come, let us deny it (deny the deposit, as a punishment for his not trusting us). He said to her: Shall we lose our trustworthiness because this fool acted improperly? So too with afflictions: at the time they are sent upon a person, they are made to swear: You shall go (to the sick person) only on such-and-such a day, and you shall leave (him) only on such-and-such a day and at such-and-such an hour, and through such-and-such (a doctor) and through such-and-such a remedy. When the time came for them to leave, this man went to a house of idol worship. The afflictions said: By right we should not leave (so that he should not think that he was healed by virtue of idolatry). Then they say: Shall we break our oath because this fool acts improperly?" And they leave at their appointed time, and those who wish to err will err.

Similarly, Rav Yehuda was asked (ibid.): There is a house of idolatry in our place, and when the world needs rain, that idol appears to the priests in a dream and says to them: Slaughter a man to me as a sacrifice and I will bring you rain. They slaughter a man to it, and the rain comes?! He answered in the name of his teacher: This is what is stated (Devarim 4:19): "which the Lord your God has allotted (ḥalak) to all the peoples under the whole heaven." Ḥalak is related to heḥlik, "made slippery": that is, God gave man free choice, so that if he wishes to choose evil, he will slip and lose his world. Therefore, one who wishes to stray after idolatry will be able to find arguments to reinforce his error and lose his world. As it is stated (Mishlei 3:34): "If it concerns the scoffers, He scoffs at them, but to the humble He gives grace": "One who comes to defile himself, the way is opened for him; one who comes to purify himself is helped."

Today, after crude idol worship has disappeared from the world through the blessed influence of the people of Israel, it is hard for us to understand how human beings believed so strongly in idols made of wood and stone. But in those days the temptation for this was immense. The Sages said (Sanhedrin 102b) that when the great Amora Rav Ashi planned to teach about Menashe, one of the wicked kings of Yehuda, he mentioned him disparagingly. In his dream at night King Menashe appeared to him, rebuked him for having disparaged his honor, and showed him the extent of his wisdom. Rav Ashi asked him: If so, why did you sin so much with idolatry? Menashe answered him: Had you lived in our generation, you would have lifted the hem of your cloak and run to worship idolatry. We indeed ran, but we did not lift the hem of our cloaks. This teaches us how strong the inclination to worship idolatry was.

The idolatrous religions, created by talented men of spirit, responded to man's natural faith and to his yearning to experience spiritual experiences and to connect to the source of power and life. For this purpose they created rites of worship that included theatrical displays of statues, song, dance, sacrifices, blood and fire, which aroused souls to undergo mighty emotional experiences. Often these experiences were intensified by rites of harlotry and human sacrifice. On the basis of the stirring experiences of idolatrous worship, it was easy to be convinced that the more sacrifices they offered to the idols and the more they participated in the rites of worshipping them, the more livelihood, health and security they would merit.

In the way of nature, many of the sick recover; but the idol worshippers who recovered imagined that they had recovered by virtue of the sacrifice they had offered to the gods in submission. And sometimes, after they had offered a sacrifice to Ba'al in a ceremony stirring to the point of losing their senses, rain fell, for in the way of nature rain falls in winter, and it seemed to people that the idol Ba'al had responded to their worship (Avoda Zara 55a). A person living, for example, in the land of Canaan, who knew that if rain did not fall on his land he and his family were liable to die of thirst and hunger, and who heard the priests of Ba'al warning that if sacrifices were not offered to Ba'al no rain would fall, even if he was not a devout believer, would be drawn after the priests of Ba'al and be willing to bring sacrifices to the priests, and in the process to participate in the worship, which included song and dancing, food and alcohol, and giving vent to his inclinations by watching ceremonies containing sexual stimulation and cruelty.

Thus, on the basis of a spiritual kernel of seeking faith and meaning in life, a social framework of immense influence was built, in which falsehood and wickedness ruled. Against all this the Torah commanded and the prophets warned that even if we should think there is truth in the words of the idol worshippers and the sorcerers, we should know that it is a test with which God tests us, for He gave people spiritual abilities, and they can turn them toward evil, in the manner of the false prophets, as it is stated (Devarim 13:2-6): "If there arises in your midst a prophet or a dreamer of dreams, and he gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass, of which he spoke to you, saying: Let us go after other gods, which you have not known, and let us serve them – you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or to that dreamer of dreams, for the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul. You shall walk after the Lord your God, and Him shall you fear, and His commandments shall you keep, and His voice shall you heed, and Him shall you serve, and to Him shall you cleave."
